title: Soap Making for Small Business: Cold-Process Bars and Simple Liquid Soap
subtitle: Make safe, correctly calculated, well-cured soap from local oils, then cost it, label it honestly and sell it.
description: A practical course for women who want to make and sell soap in Nigeria. You will handle caustic soda safely, calculate lye from SAP values and check it in SoapCalc, make cold-process bars and simple liquid soap, test and cure your products, and learn the basics of labelling, NAFDAC registration, costing and selling.
outcomes: Handle caustic soda and caustic potash safely, with correct protective equipment and first aid
Calculate caustic soda and water for any oil blend using SAP values, superfat and lye concentration, and confirm it in SoapCalc
Make, cut and cure a batch of cold-process bar soap, and mix a simple liquid wash
Test finished soap, diagnose common faults and keep complete batch records
Write an honest label and outline the NAFDAC micro-scale registration path
Cost a batch in naira, set profitable prices and plan 90 days of production and sales
audience: Women with no chemistry background who want to make quality soap at home or in a small workshop and sell it locally.
tools: Safety goggles, nitrile or rubber gloves, long sleeves
Digital kitchen scale reading in 1 g steps
Stainless steel pot, PP 5 plastic jug, silicone spatulas, stick blender, thermometer
Soap mould (lined wooden box, silicone mould or PVC pipe) and a curing rack or tray
Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide); oils such as palm oil, palm kernel oil, shea butter and castor oil; fragrance (optional)
Smartphone with SoapCalc (soapcalc.net) in the browser and WhatsApp Business

modules.title: How Soap Works, Your Ingredients and Staying Safe
modules.overview: Before you mix anything, you need to understand what soap actually is, which ingredients do which job, and how to handle caustic soda without getting hurt. This module gives you the chemistry in plain words, the vocabulary every soap maker uses, and a safe workspace you can set up at home.

lessons.title: What soap is and which kind to make first
objectives: Explain saponification in one or two plain sentences
Compare melt-and-pour, cold process, hot process and liquid soap
Choose a sensible first method for your budget and goals
Describe where handmade soap fits in the Nigerian market

blocks.text: Every true soap is made from two things: **fats or oils** and a strong alkali called **lye**. For bar soap the lye is **sodium hydroxide**, sold in Nigerian markets as caustic soda. For soft and liquid soap the lye is **potassium hydroxide**, often called caustic potash or KOH. When oil and lye meet in water, they react and turn into soap and glycerin. This reaction is called **saponification**.

blocks.name: bar-of-soap
blocks.caption: Every true bar of soap starts as oil plus caustic soda, joined by saponification.

blocks.text: Here is the simple picture. An oil molecule is like a short handle with three long tails. The lye cuts the tails off the handle. Each tail joins with sodium (or potassium) to become a soap molecule, and the handle becomes glycerin, a natural moisturiser that stays inside handmade soap. When the reaction is complete, there is no lye left in a correctly made bar. That is why careful measuring matters so much: the right amount of lye for the amount of oil.
One soap molecule, two ends

Soap cleans because each molecule has two different ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and grease. When you wash, the oil-loving ends grab dirt and grease, and the water-loving ends let the water carry it away. That is why plain water alone cannot remove palm oil from your hands, but soap and water can.
The four main ways to make soap

head: Method
What you do
Uses lye yourself?
Ready to use
rows: Buy a ready soap base, melt it, add colour and scent, pour into moulds
No, the base is already soap
Mix oils and lye solution at warm temperatures, pour, let it react in the mould
After about 4 to 6 weeks of curing
Same mix, but you cook the soap batter with heat until the reaction finishes, then pack into a mould
Usable sooner, still improves with a few weeks of drying
Cook oils with potassium hydroxide to make a paste, then dilute with water

blocks.text: Melt-and-pour is the gentlest start, because you never touch lye, but the base can be costly and hard to find in good quality, and you cannot really say you made the soap from scratch. Cold process gives you full control over ingredients and the lowest cost per bar, which is why most small soap businesses use it. Hot process uses the same recipe as cold process but finishes the reaction with heat, so the bars look more rustic.
Soap in the Nigerian setting

Soap making is not new here. Traditional African black soap, called **ose dudu** in Yoruba, is made with potash from burnt plant material such as cocoa pods or plantain peels, cooked with oils such as palm kernel oil. Today the market also has factory bars, imported "natural" bars, and many small makers selling on WhatsApp, Instagram and at local markets. The opportunity for a small maker is quality and trust: a well-made, honestly labelled bar using local oils like palm kernel oil, palm oil and shea butter.

Many people also say "liquid soap" when they mean the liquid wash for dishes and hands sold in kegs. Most of those are **liquid detergents** made from synthetic cleaning agents, not true soap. You will learn the difference and make a simple version in Module 2.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing a first method
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi lives in Enugu, has about 40,000 naira (approximate) to start, a small kitchen, and two young children at home. She wants to sell bars to friends and church members within two months.
steps: She rules out melt-and-pour as a business: a quality base would make each bar cost more than she can sell it for locally.
She chooses cold process because the oils (palm kernel oil, palm oil, shea butter) are sold in her local market.
Because of her children, she plans to make soap only when they are at school, in a corner she can lock or close off.
She counts backwards: bars need about 4 to 6 weeks to cure, so she must make her first sellable batch within the next two weeks to sell in two months.
blocks.result: Ngozi starts with cold process, makes a small test batch first, and sets a safety rule that no child is present while lye is out. Her timeline is realistic because she planned for the curing time.

blocks.title: Melt-and-pour vs cold process
items: Melt-and-pour
Cold process
blocks.caption: Cold process takes more care and time, but gives a small business control and better margins.

blocks.title: Glycerin stays in
blocks.text: Large factories often remove glycerin to sell separately. Handmade cold process soap keeps all of it, which is one honest reason customers say it feels less drying. Do not turn this into a medical claim, it is just a feature.

takeaways: Soap is oil plus lye: sodium hydroxide for bars, potassium hydroxide for liquid soap
Saponification turns oil and lye into soap and glycerin, with no lye left when measured correctly
Cold process is the usual choice for small businesses because of cost and control
Most keg "liquid soap" in markets is actually a liquid detergent

activity.title: Map your soap market
steps: Visit one market or supermarket, or check three WhatsApp or Instagram sellers near you.
Write down five soaps you see: type (factory, handmade, black soap, melt-and-pour), size, and price.
Note which ones list their ingredients and which show a NAFDAC number.
Write two sentences on which method you will start with and why.
activity.evidence: A photo of your notes or a short table of five soaps with prices, plus your two-sentence decision.

lessons.title: Oils, SAP values and the words soap makers use
objectives: Describe what each common Nigerian soap oil adds to a bar
Define SAP value, superfat, lye concentration, trace and cure
Read a simple soap recipe written in percentages
Plan a balanced oil blend from local oils

blocks.text: Every oil makes a slightly different soap. Some give a hard bar with big bubbles. Some give a gentle, creamy bar that melts quickly in a wet dish. A good recipe blends oils so the bar is hard, cleans well, lathers, and still feels kind on the skin. The good news is that the best oils for this are easy to find in Nigeria.

blocks.name: droplet
blocks.alt: A single golden drop of liquid
blocks.caption: Each oil in your blend has its own SAP value and adds its own quality to the bar.

blocks.text: Common oils and what they do

head: Oil
What it adds
Usual share of recipe
rows: Hardness, strong cleaning, big fluffy lather; can be drying if too much
Very similar to PKO: hard bar, lots of bubbles
15% to 30% (use instead of, or with, PKO)
Hard, long-lasting bar with creamy, stable lather
Very gentle, slow to trace, softer bar; costly here
Boosts and stabilises lather; makes soap sticky if too much

blocks.text: Red palm oil gives an orange to yellow bar and a natural colour customers often like. Refined palm oil and palm olein give a paler bar. Buy oils that smell fresh. Old or rancid oil can cause orange spots and a bad smell in finished soap weeks later.
The key words

items: **SAP value (saponification value):** how much lye one gram of a particular oil needs to turn fully into soap. Every oil has its own number. For example, in the SoapCalc lye calculator, coconut oil needs about 0.183 g of sodium hydroxide per gram, while palm oil needs about 0.142 g.

**Superfat:** a small amount of oil (often 5%) that you deliberately leave unreacted by using slightly less lye than the full amount. It is a safety margin, so no free lye remains, and it makes the bar milder.
**Lye concentration:** how strong your lye solution is, for example 33% means 33 g of caustic soda in every 100 g of solution. Many beginners use 30% to 33%.
**Lye solution:** caustic soda dissolved in water. It gets very hot and is the most dangerous stage.
**Trace:** the point where the oil and lye mixture thickens enough that a drizzle leaves a faint line on the surface, like thin custard. It shows the mixture has emulsified and will not separate.
**Gel phase:** the soap heats itself in the mould and may look darker and jelly-like in the middle for a while. It is normal.
**Cure:** the 4 to 6 weeks after cutting when bars dry out on a rack, becoming harder, milder and longer lasting.
**Batch record:** your written record of every batch, weights, temperatures, dates and results.

blocks.text: Reading a recipe in percentages

Soap makers write recipes as percentages of total oil weight, so the same recipe works for a small or big batch. If a recipe says palm oil 50%, and you are making 1,000 g of oils, you use 500 g. For a 2,000 g batch, you use 1,000 g. Lye and water are calculated from the oils, never guessed. You will do that calculation step by step in Module 2.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning percentages into grams
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan wants a balanced bar from local oils and plans a test batch of 800 g of oils.
steps: Her recipe: palm oil 50%, palm kernel oil 30%, shea butter 15%, castor oil 5%. The percentages add up to 100%.
Palm oil: 800 x 0.50 = 400 g.
Palm kernel oil: 800 x 0.30 = 240 g.
Shea butter: 800 x 0.15 = 120 g.
blocks.result: Bisi has exact gram weights for each oil. She will enter the same percentages into a lye calculator to get the exact caustic soda and water for 800 g of oils.

blocks.title: Building a balanced oil blend
items: Castor: lather booster
Shea: conditioning
PKO or coconut: cleansing
Palm oil: hard base
blocks.caption: Start with a hard base oil, add a cleansing oil, then smaller amounts of conditioning and lather oils.

blocks.text: Weigh everything, including oils. Do not measure oil in cups or bottles, because a litre of oil does not weigh 1,000 g and different oils have different weights. Melt solid oils such as shea butter and palm kernel oil gently before weighing them into the pot, and always zero (tare) the scale with the empty container on it first. Write each weight down as you go, so you never have to remember whether you already added the castor oil.

blocks.title: Keep it simple at first
blocks.text: Three or four oils are enough. Changing many oils at once makes it hard to know what caused a problem. Change one thing per batch and write it in your batch record.

takeaways: Each oil has its own SAP value, so lye is always calculated, never guessed
Superfat of about 5% is a safety margin and makes the bar milder
Recipes are percentages of oil weight, so they scale up or down easily
Palm oil, palm kernel oil and shea butter make a good local base

activity.title: Design your first oil blend
steps: Price palm oil, palm kernel oil, shea butter and castor oil at your nearest market and note the prices.
Write a four-oil recipe in percentages that adds up to 100%, using the ranges in the table.
Convert it to grams for a 1,000 g batch.
Write one sentence on what kind of bar you expect (hard, bubbly, creamy) and why.
activity.evidence: Your recipe card with percentages, grams and market prices (photo or note).

lessons.title: Caustic soda safety and setting up your workspace
objectives: List the protective equipment needed before handling lye
Mix a lye solution in the safe order and place
Give correct first aid for lye on skin, in eyes or swallowed
Set up and store tools so children and others are protected

blocks.text: Caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) is a strong alkali. It burns skin and can blind you if it splashes in your eyes. It does not always sting at once, so you may not notice a burn until it is serious. Treat it with the same respect you would give boiling oil. With the right habits, thousands of small makers handle it safely every day.

blocks.name: goggles
blocks.caption: Sealed goggles go on before the caustic soda container is ever opened.

blocks.text: Protective equipment (non-negotiable)

items: **Safety goggles** that seal around the eyes. Ordinary glasses are not enough.
**Rubber or nitrile gloves** that cover your wrists.
**Long sleeves, long trousers or wrapper, and closed shoes.** An apron helps.
**Good ventilation:** mix lye outdoors or by an open window with a fan pushing air out. The solution gives off strong fumes for about a minute; do not breathe them.
**A face mask** is helpful when weighing powdery caustic soda.

blocks.text: The right tools and the wrong ones

Use **stainless steel** pots and spoons, or heavy plastic marked with recycling number **5 (PP)**, which handles the heat. **Never use aluminium**, tin or zinc: lye attacks them and releases hydrogen gas. Avoid thin glass, which can crack from the sudden heat. Use a **digital kitchen scale** that reads in 1 g steps, a thermometer (an infrared or probe thermometer), a stick (immersion) blender, silicone spatulas, and a mould (wooden box lined with paper, silicone mould, or a cut PVC pipe). Keep all soap tools for soap only, never for food again.
Mixing lye safely

items: Put on goggles, gloves and long sleeves. Make sure children and pets are out of the room.
Weigh cold water (distilled, or clean boiled and cooled water) into a heat-safe container.
Weigh caustic soda into a separate dry container.
In a ventilated spot, **slowly pour the caustic soda into the water**, stirring gently. **Never pour water onto caustic soda**, it can boil up and splash violently.
Step back from the fumes. The solution heats up fast and can pass 80 degrees Celsius.
Label it "LYE, DO NOT TOUCH" and leave it to cool somewhere no one can knock it over.

blocks.title: First aid you must know before you start
blocks.text: **On skin:** remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of cool running water for at least 15 minutes. Do not use vinegar on the skin; water is the correct first treatment. **In the eyes:** rinse immediately with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, and go to a hospital straight away. **Swallowed:** rinse the mouth, do not make the person vomit, and get medical help immediately. Keep a clean jug or bottle of water on the table every time you work.
Storing caustic soda

Caustic soda pulls water from the air, which matters in humid places like Lagos or Port Harcourt. Keep it in its original sealed container or a tightly closed, clearly labelled plastic jar, on a high shelf or locked cupboard. Never store it in a drink bottle or food container, because a child or adult could mistake it for something else. Buy sealed, labelled flakes or pearls from a trusted chemical seller; old or damp soda gives unpredictable results.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up a kitchen corner
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna shares a kitchen with her sister and wants a safe soap corner without buying much.
steps: She chooses a table next to the back door so she can mix lye outside on the step and work with the door open.
She buys goggles (about 2,500 naira, approximate), a box of nitrile gloves (about 3,500 naira, approximate) and a digital scale (about 6,000 naira, approximate).
She labels a stainless pot, a PP 5 jug and two spatulas "SOAP ONLY" in marker and keeps them in a separate carton.
She writes the first aid steps on a card and tapes it to the wall above the table, with a 2 litre bottle of water beside it.
She agrees with her sister that no one cooks food in the kitchen while lye is out.
blocks.result: With about 12,000 naira (approximate) of safety equipment and clear rules, Halima has a workspace that protects her and her household before she makes a single bar.

blocks.title: Before you open the caustic soda
items: Goggles, gloves, long sleeves on
Children and pets out
Ventilation open
Water ready for first aid
No aluminium tools
blocks.caption: Run through these five checks every single time, even when you feel experienced.

blocks.title: Spills and waste
blocks.text: Sweep up dry caustic soda spills with a dustpan while wearing gloves, then wipe the area with plenty of water. Pour small amounts of leftover lye solution slowly into a drain with lots of running water, never onto soil where children play.

takeaways: Goggles, gloves and long sleeves every time lye is out
Always add caustic soda to water, never water to caustic soda
Rinse lye splashes with running water for at least 15 minutes; eyes need hospital care
Use stainless steel or PP 5 plastic, never aluminium
Store caustic soda sealed, labelled and out of children's reach

activity.title: Build your safety station
steps: Collect or price goggles, gloves, a digital scale, a stainless pot and a PP 5 jug.
Choose your work spot and check it has ventilation and a place to put lye out of reach.
Write the first aid steps on a card and place it at your work spot.
Label every soap tool "SOAP ONLY".
activity.evidence: A photo of your safety station with goggles, gloves, scale and the first aid card visible.

quiz.q: Hauwa is about to mix her lye solution. Which order is correct?
options: Pour water onto the caustic soda in a closed room
Slowly pour caustic soda into water in a ventilated place
Mix caustic soda into warm oil first
Pour both into the mould at the same time
quiz.explain: Caustic soda always goes into water, slowly, with ventilation. Water poured onto caustic soda can boil up and splash.

quiz.q: A drop of lye solution splashes onto Ada's arm. What should she do first?
options: Rinse with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes
Wipe it with a dry cloth and continue
quiz.explain: Running water for at least 15 minutes is the correct first treatment. Vinegar is not recommended on skin.

quiz.q: What does a 5% superfat mean?
options: 5% extra lye is added for hardness
About 5% of the oils are left unreacted as a safety margin
The soap must cure for 5 weeks
quiz.explain: Superfat means using slightly less lye than needed so a little oil remains, making the bar milder and safer.

quiz.q: Which pot should Chioma NOT use for soap making?
quiz.explain: Lye reacts with aluminium and releases hydrogen gas. Use stainless steel or PP 5 plastic.

quiz.q: A recipe uses palm oil 40%. How much palm oil goes into a 1,500 g oil batch?
quiz.explain: 1,500 x 0.40 = 600 g. Recipes are percentages of total oil weight.

modules.title: Making Your First Batches: Bar Soap, Lye Calculation and Liquid Soap
modules.overview: Now you make soap. You will follow the full cold-process method, calculate caustic soda and water from SAP values with a fully worked example, check it with the free SoapCalc calculator, and learn two routes to liquid soap: true potash soap and the simple liquid wash sold in kegs.

lessons.title: Cold-process bar soap, step by step
objectives: Prepare oils and lye solution at the right temperatures
Bring a batch to trace with a stick blender
Pour, insulate, unmould and cut a batch safely
Set bars up for a proper 4 to 6 week cure

blocks.text: This lesson walks through one complete batch. Read it all the way through before you start, and have your recipe, already calculated, written on paper beside you. You will learn the calculation in the next lesson; for your very first batch you can use the worked recipe in Lesson 2.2, which has been checked.

blocks.name: thermometer
blocks.caption: Recording lye and oil temperatures, roughly 35 to 45 degrees Celsius, keeps each batch predictable.

blocks.text: Stage 1: Prepare

items: Put on goggles, gloves and long sleeves. Clear the table. Children and pets out.
Line your mould with baking paper if it is wooden or plastic. Silicone moulds need no lining.
Weigh and gently melt the solid oils (palm kernel oil, palm oil, shea butter) in your stainless pot over low heat. Take it off the heat as soon as everything is liquid.
Weigh and add the liquid oils (such as castor oil) to the melted oils.
Weigh your fragrance or essential oil into a small glass or PP cup and set it aside.

blocks.text: Stage 2: Make and cool the lye solution

Weigh the water, then the caustic soda, and slowly add the caustic soda to the water in a ventilated place, stirring until clear. Let it cool. Many beginners aim to combine when both the lye solution and the oils are between about **35 and 45 degrees Celsius**. Cooler mixing gives you more time; hotter mixing traces faster. Write both temperatures in your batch record.
Stage 3: Bring to trace

items: Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils down the shaft of the stick blender, to avoid splashes and air bubbles.
With the blender switched off, stir with it for a few seconds. Then pulse the blender for 3 to 5 seconds, stir, and repeat.
Stop when you reach light trace: a drizzle from the spatula leaves a faint line on the surface before sinking. This usually takes a few minutes with a blender. By hand it can take a very long time.
Add the fragrance and stir it in by hand or with a short pulse. Some fragrances speed up trace, so be ready to pour.

blocks.text: Stage 4: Pour, rest, cut

items: Pour the batter into the mould and tap it on the table to release air bubbles.
Cover with a piece of cardboard and, if you want a full gel phase, a towel. In hot weather, many makers skip the towel to avoid overheating.
Leave it undisturbed for 24 to 48 hours, away from children. The soap is still caustic during this time.
Wearing gloves, unmould and cut into bars with a sharp knife or soap cutter. If it is too soft to cut cleanly, wait another day.
Place bars on a rack or clean tray with space between them, in a cool, airy place out of direct sun, for 4 to 6 weeks. Turn them every few days.

blocks.title: Raw soap batter is still caustic
blocks.text: Until the reaction finishes, the batter and fresh soap can burn skin. Keep gloves on while pouring, unmoulding and cutting. Do not let anyone touch the fresh soap, and do not lick or taste anything.
If something looks wrong on the day

items: **Batter thickens suddenly and becomes lumpy (seizing):** often caused by some fragrance oils or mixing too hot. Work fast, press it into the mould, and note the fragrance in your record.
**Oil pools on top and will not trace after a long time:** check that you weighed the caustic soda correctly. If you are not sure, do not sell this batch.
**Batter thickens in seconds when you first blend:** it may be false trace from solid oils cooling. Check the temperature; warm oils slightly next time.
**Cracks or a dark wet patch on top after a day:** the soap overheated. In hot weather, skip the towel and keep the mould in a cool room.

blocks.text: Clean-up

Wipe excess batter from tools with paper towels while wearing gloves, and put the paper in a bag in the bin. Many makers leave the pot covered for a day: the leftover batter turns into soap and washes off easily with hot water. Wash lye containers separately with plenty of water.

blocks.title: Worked example: one batch timeline
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Lagos makes her first 1,000 g oil batch on a Saturday morning using the recipe from Lesson 2.2.
steps: 8:00 am: safety gear on, mould lined, oils weighed and melted. Lye solution mixed on the balcony at 8:20.
9:10 am: lye solution 42 degrees Celsius, oils 40 degrees Celsius. She combines them.
9:16 am: light trace after about 6 minutes of pulsing. She adds 30 g of fragrance oil and pours at 9:18.
Monday 9:00 am: soap is firm. She unmoulds and cuts 10 bars, each about 140 g.
She writes the cut date and "ready from" date (5 weeks later) on a label on the drying tray.
blocks.result: Amaka has 10 bars curing, a full batch record with times and temperatures, and a clear date when the soap can be tested and sold.

blocks.title: Cold-process workflow
items: Prepare oils and mould
Mix and cool lye
Blend to light trace
Pour and insulate
Cut after 24 to 48 hours
Cure 4 to 6 weeks
blocks.caption: Each stage has its own safety step; never skip curing, even if a customer is waiting.

takeaways: Have your calculated recipe written down before you start
Combine lye and oils when both are roughly 35 to 45 degrees Celsius, and record the temperatures
Pulse and stir to light trace, then add fragrance and pour
Fresh soap is still caustic: gloves on until it is cut and curing
Cure bars 4 to 6 weeks in a cool, airy place

activity.title: Make a small test batch
steps: Copy the recipe from Lesson 2.2 (or your own checked recipe) onto a batch record sheet.
Run the five safety checks from Lesson 1.3.
Make the batch, writing down times, temperatures and how long trace took.
Unmould, cut and set the bars to cure, labelled with the date.
activity.evidence: Your completed batch record plus photos of the poured mould and the cut bars on the curing rack.

lessons.title: Calculating caustic soda and water with SAP values and SoapCalc
objectives: Calculate the caustic soda needed for any oil blend using SAP values
Apply a superfat and work out water from a lye concentration
Enter a recipe into SoapCalc and read the result
Check your answer against a second calculation before making soap

blocks.text: Getting the lye amount right is what makes soap safe. Too much caustic soda leaves a harsh, burning bar. Too little leaves a greasy, soft bar that may go rancid. You will learn the calculation by hand so you understand it, then use a free lye calculator so you never rely on your arithmetic alone.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working out figures on a large calculator
blocks.caption: Calculate lye by hand from SAP values, then confirm the answer in SoapCalc.

blocks.text: The formula

items: **Lye for each oil** = weight of oil (g) x SAP value of that oil (sodium hydroxide).
**Total lye at 0% superfat** = add the lye for all the oils.
**Lye with superfat** = total lye x (1 minus superfat). For 5% superfat, multiply by 0.95.
**Water from lye concentration** = lye divided by concentration, minus the lye. For 33% concentration: lye / 0.33 minus lye.

blocks.text: SAP values used in this course

head: Oil
Sodium hydroxide per g of oil (bar soap)
Potassium hydroxide per g of oil (liquid soap)

blocks.text: These figures are the values listed in the SoapCalc calculator. Other calculators may use slightly different numbers, so your answers may differ by a gram or two. That is normal and covered by the superfat. A big difference means a mistake.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 1,000 g palm, PKO and shea bar
blocks.context: For example, Amaka plans 1,000 g of oils: palm oil 500 g (50%), palm kernel oil 300 g (30%), shea butter 150 g (15%), castor oil 50 g (5%). She wants 5% superfat and a 33% lye concentration.
steps: Palm oil: 500 x 0.142 = 71.0 g of caustic soda.
Palm kernel oil: 300 x 0.176 = 52.8 g.
Shea butter: 150 x 0.128 = 19.2 g.
Castor oil: 50 x 0.128 = 6.4 g.
With 5% superfat: 149.4 x 0.95 = 141.9 g of caustic soda.
Water at 33% concentration: 141.9 / 0.33 = 430.0 g of solution; 430.0 minus 141.9 = 288.1 g of water.
Fragrance at 3% of oils: 1,000 x 0.03 = 30 g.
blocks.result: Amaka weighs 142 g of caustic soda and 288 g of water. Her total batch is about 1,000 + 142 + 288 + 30 = 1,460 g of soap batter, enough for about 10 bars of 140 g.

blocks.text: Water: how much is enough?

Water only carries the lye into the oils and evaporates during curing. It does not change how much lye you need. A 33% lye concentration is a comfortable middle for beginners. More water (for example SoapCalc's default of 38% of oil weight, which for 1,000 g of oils is 380 g) gives a slower trace and more time to work, but a softer bar at first and a longer cure. Less water (stronger solution, up to about 40%) traces faster and can overheat. Stay between 30% and 35% until you have made several good batches.
Scaling up

Because the recipe is in percentages, scaling is easy. To make 3,000 g of oils from Amaka's recipe, multiply every oil, the caustic soda and the water by 3: about 426 g of caustic soda and 864 g of water. Still re-run the calculator with the new oil weight. A big batch heats up more, so watch the temperature and do not insulate as heavily.

blocks.title: About rounding
blocks.text: Round caustic soda to the nearest whole gram on a 1 g scale, and never round up the lye by more than a gram. Rounding down slightly just increases the superfat a little, which is the safer direction.
Using SoapCalc (soapcalc.net)

items: Open soapcalc.net on your phone or computer and choose the lye calculator.
Select NaOH (sodium hydroxide) for bar soap.
Enter the weight of oils (1,000 g) and choose grams.
For water, choose lye concentration and enter 33%, or keep water as a percentage of oils.
Enter superfat 5% and fragrance ratio if you want it calculated.
Add each oil from the list and type its percentage. Check the total shows 100%.
Calculate, then open the printable recipe and compare its caustic soda and water with your hand calculation.

blocks.text: SoapCalc also shows soap quality numbers such as hardness, cleansing and conditioning. They are helpful guides, but the lye and water weights are what keep you safe. Save a screenshot or printout of every recipe in your batch records.

blocks.title: From oils to a safe lye amount
items: Weigh each oil
Multiply by its SAP
Add the totals
Apply 5% superfat
Work out water
Check in SoapCalc
blocks.caption: Two independent calculations that agree within a gram or two give you confidence to make the batch.

blocks.title: Never swap lye types
blocks.text: Sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide have different SAP values. A recipe calculated for one cannot be made with the other. If a recipe from the internet does not say which lye it uses, or you cannot recalculate it, do not use it.

takeaways: Lye = oil weight x SAP value, added up for all oils
Multiply by 0.95 for a 5% superfat
Water at 33% concentration = lye / 0.33 minus lye
Always check your hand calculation in a lye calculator before mixing

activity.title: Calculate your own recipe
steps: Take the oil blend you designed in Lesson 1.2 and convert it to grams for 1,000 g.
Calculate caustic soda at 5% superfat and water at 33% concentration by hand, showing each line.
Enter the same recipe into SoapCalc and screenshot the result.
Write down the difference between your answer and SoapCalc and explain it in one sentence.
activity.evidence: Your handwritten calculation and the SoapCalc screenshot side by side.

lessons.title: Simple liquid soap: true potash soap and the keg liquid wash
objectives: Explain the difference between true liquid soap and liquid detergent
Calculate potassium hydroxide for a small liquid soap batch
Mix a simple SLES liquid wash safely and thicken it with salt
Choose safe preservatives and avoid hazardous shortcuts

blocks.text: There are two very different products people call liquid soap. **True liquid soap** is real soap made from oils and **potassium hydroxide** (caustic potash, KOH), which makes soft, water-soluble soap. **Liquid detergent** (the common keg dish and hand wash) is made from synthetic cleaning agents such as **SLES** (sodium laureth sulfate, often sold as "texapon"). Both can be good products. You must label each honestly.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.alt: A pump bottle of liquid soap
blocks.caption: Liquid soap and liquid wash go into clean, labelled pump bottles with a batch number.

blocks.title: Two kinds of liquid soap
items: True liquid soap
Liquid detergent wash
right: No lye if made this way
blocks.caption: Choose the route that fits your customers, and name the product honestly on the label.

blocks.text: Route 1: True liquid soap with potassium hydroxide

The method is like hot process: oils and a potassium hydroxide solution are blended and cooked gently until they become a thick, translucent paste. The paste is then dissolved in hot water to the thickness you want. The safety rules for caustic soda apply in full to caustic potash. Liquid soap makers usually use a very low superfat, often 0% to 3%, because extra oil makes the liquid cloudy.
Commercial potassium hydroxide is often not 100% pure; around 90% is common. Lye calculators let you enter the purity. Always check what your supplier states on the label or certificate.

blocks.title: Worked example: potassium hydroxide for a 500 g oil batch
blocks.context: For example, Funmi in Abeokuta wants to try true liquid soap with 400 g coconut oil and 100 g castor oil, a 3% superfat, and potassium hydroxide labelled 90% pure.
steps: Coconut oil: 400 x 0.257 = 102.8 g of pure potassium hydroxide.
Castor oil: 100 x 0.180 = 18.0 g.
Total at 0% superfat: 120.8 g.
With 3% superfat: 120.8 x 0.97 = 117.2 g.
Adjust for 90% purity: 117.2 / 0.90 = 130.2 g of the potash she bought.
She enters the same recipe in SoapCalc with KOH selected to confirm before mixing.
blocks.result: Funmi weighs about 130 g of her 90% potassium hydroxide. After cooking, she dilutes the paste with water a little at a time, recording the ratio of paste to water that gives the thickness she wants.

blocks.text: Route 2: A simple SLES liquid wash

SLES is usually sold as a thick paste of about 70% active cleaning agent. You dilute it with clean water, then thicken it with ordinary salt. This route needs no caustic soda at all, which makes it safer than recipes that use sulphonic acid, a corrosive acid that must be neutralised with caustic soda or soda ash. This course does not teach the sulphonic acid route.

items: Wear gloves and goggles: SLES paste irritates eyes and skin.
Decide the active level. About 10% active is a reasonable starting point for a dish wash; you can test higher or lower.
Dissolve the SLES paste slowly in part of the water, stirring gently to avoid too much foam. Leave it to dissolve fully, even overnight.
Add the rest of the water, then colour and fragrance in small amounts.
Dissolve salt in a little water and add it bit by bit, stirring and checking thickness. Stop when it is thick enough. Too much salt makes it thin again.
Add a cosmetic preservative at the rate the supplier states, then fill clean, labelled bottles.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 10 kg dish wash
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Benin City wants 10 kg of dish wash at about 10% active, using 70% SLES paste.
steps: Active needed: 10 kg x 0.10 = 1.0 kg of active SLES.
Paste needed: 1.0 / 0.70 = 1.43 kg of 70% SLES paste.
She dissolves the paste in about 4 kg of water and leaves it overnight.
She adds water to bring the total close to 10 kg, then adds salt solution 50 g of salt at a time until it thickens, recording the total salt used.
She adds colour, fragrance and preservative, then weighs to confirm about 10 kg.
blocks.result: Grace has about 10 kg of liquid wash with a known active level and a written record of how much salt she used, so the next batch will be the same.

blocks.text: Testing and bottling liquid products

Before selling, test each new recipe for a week. Leave a filled bottle on a shelf and check daily for separation, cloudiness, a change in smell or mould. Use clean, dry bottles with tight caps, and fill to the same weight every time so customers get what the label says. Write a batch number on every bottle. If a customer complains, the batch number lets you find your record and see exactly what went into that bottle.

blocks.title: Avoid formalin as a preservative
blocks.text: Some local recipes add formalin (formaldehyde solution) as a preservative. Formaldehyde is classified as a cancer-causing substance by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. Use a cosmetic preservative sold for this purpose, at the supplier's stated rate, and keep all water-based products in clean containers.

takeaways: True liquid soap uses potassium hydroxide; keg liquid wash is usually a detergent
Adjust potassium hydroxide for purity: pure amount divided by 0.90 for 90% KOH
SLES wash is diluted to a chosen active level and thickened with salt in small steps
Water-based products need a proper preservative, never formalin

activity.title: Make a 1 kg liquid wash test
steps: Scale Grace's recipe to 1 kg: work out the SLES paste needed for 10% active.
Mix it with gloves and goggles on, adding salt in 5 g steps and recording each addition.
Test it on a few greasy plates and note foam, grease removal and how it feels on hands.
Label the bottle with name, ingredients, batch number and date.
activity.evidence: Your mixing record with salt amounts, a photo of the labelled bottle, and your test notes.

quiz.q: A recipe has 400 g palm oil (SAP 0.142). How much caustic soda does the palm oil need at 0% superfat?
quiz.explain: 400 x 0.142 = 56.8 g. Each oil's weight is multiplied by its own SAP value.

quiz.q: The total caustic soda for Ifeoma's recipe is 160 g at 0% superfat. What is it at 5% superfat?
quiz.explain: 160 x 0.95 = 152 g. Superfat reduces the lye, never increases it.

quiz.q: Her soap batter is at light trace. What should she do next?
options: Add fragrance, stir in, and pour into the mould
quiz.explain: At light trace, add fragrance and pour. Over-blending makes it too thick to pour smoothly.

quiz.q: Kemi kept adding salt to her SLES dish wash. It thickened, then turned thin again. What happened?
options: Too much salt can make SLES thin again
quiz.explain: Salt thickens SLES up to a point; beyond it, the liquid becomes thin again. Add salt in small steps and record it.

quiz.q: Funmi needs 117 g of pure potassium hydroxide, but her KOH is 90% pure. How much should she weigh?
quiz.explain: 117 / 0.90 = 130 g. Impure lye contains less active alkali, so more of it is needed.

quiz.q: Amaka's hand calculation gives 142 g of caustic soda; SoapCalc gives 141 g. What should she do?
options: Proceed: a 1 g difference is normal
quiz.explain: Small differences come from slightly different SAP values. A big gap would signal a mistake.

modules.title: Quality, Honest Labelling and NAFDAC Basics
modules.overview: A bar is only ready to sell when it is safe, consistent and honestly labelled. This module shows you how to cure and test soap, recognise and fix common faults, label without false claims, understand the basic NAFDAC registration path for small producers, and keep records that prove your quality.

lessons.title: Curing, testing and fixing common soap faults
objectives: Judge when a bar has cured using weight and feel
Test finished soap with pH strips
Recognise common faults and decide whether a batch is safe to sell
Trace a fault back to its likely cause in your batch record

blocks.text: Fresh soap is not finished soap. In the first day or two, saponification completes in the mould. Over the next weeks, water slowly evaporates. The bar becomes harder, milder, and lasts longer in the soap dish. That is why cold-process soap is cured for **4 to 6 weeks** before selling. Selling early may bring quick money but leads to soft bars that melt away and disappointed customers.

blocks.name: test-tube
blocks.caption: A simple pH strip test, around pH 9 to 10, tells you whether a cured bar is ready.

blocks.title: From pour to sale
items: Day 0: pour
Day 1 to 2: unmould, cut
Weeks 1 to 4: drying
Week 4 to 6: test
Then label and sell
blocks.caption: Plan production backwards from the date you want to sell, adding at least 4 to 6 weeks.

blocks.text: How to know a bar is cured

items: **Weight test:** mark three bars from each batch and weigh them every week. When the weight stops dropping noticeably from one week to the next, most of the water has gone.
**Feel test:** a cured bar feels hard and does not dent easily with a fingernail.
**Use test:** wash your hands with one bar. It should lather well and leave skin feeling clean, not tight or stinging.

blocks.text: Where and how to cure

Cure bars on a rack, a clean wooden shelf or a plastic tray lined with baking paper, with a finger's width of space between bars so air reaches every side. Choose a cool room out of direct sun, away from the kitchen stove and from damp bathroom air. A ceiling fan on low helps in humid months. Avoid covering the bars with nylon during cure, because it traps moisture. Keep curing soap where children cannot reach it, and label the tray with the batch number and the date the bars will be ready. Turn bars every few days so the bottom dries as well as the top.
pH testing

All true soap is alkaline. Well-made handmade soap usually tests at about **pH 9 to 10** on pH strips. Wet a small area of the bar, rub to make a little lather, and press a strip into it. Compare the colour with the chart on the packet. A reading clearly above 10, especially with stinging on the skin, suggests too much lye. Do not sell that batch; check your batch record and calculation. pH strips are cheap and sold online and in some laboratory shops. Some old-school makers touch soap to the tongue (the "zap test"); pH strips are a safer habit.
Common faults and what to do

head: What you see
Likely cause
Safe to sell?
rows: White powder on the top surface (soda ash)
Lye on the surface reacting with air before saponification finished
Yes, once cured. Trim or wash it off for looks. Cover the mould next time
White, crunchy or hard pockets inside the bar
Undissolved caustic soda or poor mixing
Oily layer or soft greasy patches
Too little lye, weighing error, or not mixed to trace
No, unless you are sure of the cause. Check your record
Orange or brown spots appearing weeks later
Old or rancid oils, or too much superfat
Usually safe but looks and smells bad. Use fresher oils
Soft bar that will not harden
Too much soft oil, too much water, or not cured long enough
Cure longer and retest; reformulate next time
Cracks or a tunnel in the middle
Usually yes if pH is fine; insulate less next time
Glycerin pulling moisture from humid air
Yes. Store in a drier place, wrap after cure

blocks.title: Worked example: diagnosing a soft batch
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Owerri finds her bars still soft after 5 weeks while her friend's bars from the same week are hard.
steps: She weighs three bars: 132 g, 131 g and 131 g, the same as last week, so they are dry.
She tests the pH: about 9. The bars do not sting.
She checks her batch record: she used 40% olive oil and only 10% palm kernel oil, with no palm oil.
She enters the recipe into SoapCalc and sees the hardness number is low compared with her friend's palm and PKO recipe.
blocks.result: The batch is safe but soft. Esther sells it cheaply as a gentle bar to family, and reformulates with 40% palm oil and 25% palm kernel oil for the next batch.

blocks.text: Most faults come from three places: weighing, temperature and ingredients. Weighing errors are the most serious, so the habits from Module 2 (write every weight, use a 1 g scale, check the recipe in a calculator) prevent most dangerous batches. Temperature problems usually only affect looks. Ingredient problems, such as rancid oil or a fragrance that speeds up trace, show up as spots, smells or seizing, and your batch record tells you which supplier to question.

blocks.title: When in doubt, do not sell
blocks.text: If you are not sure whether a batch has excess lye, do not sell it or give it away. Dispose of it wearing gloves. Your reputation depends on every bar being safe.

takeaways: Cure cold-process soap 4 to 6 weeks; weigh bars weekly to confirm
Handmade soap usually tests around pH 9 to 10; clearly higher means investigate
Soda ash is cosmetic; white crunchy pockets or oily patches mean do not sell
Use your batch record to trace every fault back to a cause

activity.title: Run a cure and quality check
steps: Mark three bars from your test batch and weigh them once a week, writing the weights down.
At week 4 or later, test one bar with a pH strip and note the reading.
Check every bar for the faults in the table and note any you find.
Decide: sell, use at home, or discard, and write why.
activity.evidence: A weight log for three bars, a photo of the pH strip against its colour chart, and your sell or discard decision.

lessons.title: Honest labels, safe claims and NAFDAC basics
objectives: Write a soap label with ingredients, weight, batch and contact details
Avoid medical claims that a cosmetic should not make
Describe the NAFDAC registration path for a micro-scale soap maker
List the documents you need to start preparing now

blocks.text: Customers trust a label. A clear, honest label shows you are a serious producer, helps people with sensitive skin choose safely, and is a step toward registration with NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control), the body that regulates cosmetics, soaps and detergents in Nigeria.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: An honest label lists ingredients, net weight, batch number, dates and your contact details.

blocks.text: What to put on your label

items: Product name and type (for example "Shea and Palm Bar Soap").

**Ingredients**, from largest to smallest. Handmade soap makers often list saponified oils by their international (INCI) names, such as Sodium Palmate (palm oil soap), Sodium Palm Kernelate, Sodium Shea Butterate and Sodium Castorate, plus Water, Glycerin and Fragrance.
**Net weight** after curing, for example 120 g. Weigh cured bars, not fresh ones.
Your business name, address and phone number.
**Batch number**, date of manufacture and a best-before or expiry date.
Simple directions and a caution, for example "For external use. Avoid contact with eyes."
Your NAFDAC registration number, once you have one.

blocks.text: Check NAFDAC's current labelling requirements for cosmetics before printing a large stock of labels, because regulators update them.
Use a label size that fits your wrap, print it clearly in a font large enough to read, and keep a copy of every label version in your records so you know which batches carried which wording.
Claims you must not make

Soap is a cosmetic: it cleans and can make skin feel soft. Saying a soap **treats or cures** a disease, such as "cures eczema", "kills infection" or "clears acne", is a medicinal claim. Drugs are regulated separately and more strictly. Stick to what you can honestly say: the oils you used, that it is handmade, the scent, and how it feels. Avoid "100% chemical free" too: everything, including water and soap, is a chemical, and every true soap was made with lye.

blocks.title: Allergens and fragrance
blocks.text: Some people react to fragrance and essential oils. List fragrance on the label and offer an unscented bar. Use fragrance only up to the supplier's stated maximum for soap, and never add bleaching agents or medicines to soap.
NAFDAC registration: the basic path

NAFDAC's guidelines for cosmetics made in Nigeria state that no cosmetic should be manufactured, sold or distributed in Nigeria unless it is registered. NAFDAC has a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) route. Its MSME page describes micro businesses as those with fewer than 10 employees, and lists soaps, laundry detergents and shea butter among the cosmetic products that can be registered at micro scale. Not more than five products can be registered under micro scale.

blocks.title: Micro-scale NAFDAC path
items: Register business name with CAC
Prepare site and documents
Apply on registration.nafdac.gov.ng
Inspection and sample analysis
Approval and NAFDAC number
blocks.caption: Start with CAC registration and a clean, organised production site; everything else builds on those.

items: **Business registration:** NAFDAC accepts evidence of a registered business name for MSMEs (from the Corporate Affairs Commission, CAC).
**Online application:** through the NAFDAC e-registration portal at registration.nafdac.gov.ng.

**Supporting items** listed by NAFDAC for micro scale include CAC registration, a site agreement, product samples and a fumigation certificate; trademark approval is listed as optional at micro scale.
**Inspection:** NAFDAC inspects the production site for good manufacturing practice.
**Labels and analysis:** your label artwork is reviewed and product samples are analysed.
**Validity:** NAFDAC's MSME page states a micro-scale listing certificate is valid for 2 years; full cosmetic registration certificates are valid for 5 years.

blocks.text: NAFDAC's MSME page lists a fee for micro-scale cosmetics (41,000 naira at the time of writing). Fees change, so confirm the current amount on the NAFDAC website or at the nearest NAFDAC office before you budget. Pay only through official NAFDAC channels and be careful of agents promising a number in days.

blocks.title: Worked example: a label and a document plan
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin sells to neighbours and wants to reach supermarkets within a year.
steps: She writes her label: "Rukky's Shea and Palm Bar. Ingredients: Sodium Palmate, Sodium Palm Kernelate, Aqua (Water), Sodium Shea Butterate, Glycerin, Sodium Castorate, Fragrance. Net weight 120 g. Batch RK-003. Made 02/03, best before 02/03 next year. For external use. Avoid eyes." plus her phone number and address.
She removes the line "heals rashes" from her draft label.
She registers her business name with CAC, budgeting for the CAC fee and NAFDAC fee after checking current amounts.
She separates soap production from cooking in a clean room with shelves, and starts a file of batch records for inspection.
blocks.result: Rukayat's label is honest and complete, and she has a step-by-step plan toward a NAFDAC listing instead of waiting until a supermarket asks for a number.

blocks.title: Check the source yourself
blocks.text: Rules and fees change. Read NAFDAC's MSME page and its cosmetics guidelines on nafdac.gov.ng, or visit a NAFDAC office, before you apply.

takeaways: Labels need ingredients, net weight, maker details, batch number and dates
Never claim soap treats or cures a disease
NAFDAC has a micro-scale route that covers soaps and detergents
Start with CAC business name registration and a clean, recorded production site
Confirm current fees and requirements directly with NAFDAC

activity.title: Draft your label and registration checklist
steps: Write a full label for your test soap using the list in this lesson.
Remove any words that sound like a medical claim.
Visit nafdac.gov.ng (MSME page) and note the current micro-scale requirements and fee.
Write a dated checklist of documents you still need, starting with CAC.
activity.evidence: Your draft label (photo or file) and your dated NAFDAC readiness checklist.

lessons.title: Batch records and the numbers that show quality
objectives: Keep a complete batch record for every batch
Calculate yield, reject rate and cure weight loss
Use your records to improve the next batch
Write a short quality report another person can follow

blocks.text: A batch record is the written story of one batch. It protects your customers, because you can trace any problem. It protects you, because you can show NAFDAC inspectors, buyers or a supermarket that you work carefully. And it makes you better, because you can see exactly what changed between a good batch and a bad one.

blocks.name: ledger
blocks.caption: A batch record book lets you trace every bar back to its recipe, temperatures and test results.

blocks.text: What a batch record contains

head: Section
What to write
rows: Batch number (for example RK-004), date, your name
Each oil and its weight, caustic soda, water, superfat, lye concentration, fragrance and colour, with supplier names
Lye and oil temperatures, time to trace, any problems (seizing, overheating)
Number of bars cut, weight of three marked bars at cutting
Weekly weights of the marked bars, pH test result and date
Sold, used at home or discarded, and why
One thing to keep, one thing to change

blocks.text: You can keep this in a hard-cover notebook, a printed sheet in a file, or a simple spreadsheet in Google Sheets on your phone. Whatever you choose, use the same format every time and back up photos of the pages, for example in a WhatsApp chat with yourself or a cloud folder.
Records for supplies, not only batches

Keep a simple purchase log too: date, item, supplier, quantity, price paid and any batch or lot number on the container. When a batch goes wrong, you can see whether it shared a new keg of palm oil or a new bag of caustic soda with other problem batches. The purchase log also feeds your costing in Module 4, because it shows exactly what each gram of oil costs you today, not what it cost three months ago.

Store your caustic soda receipts and supplier details with these records. If NAFDAC inspects your site, being able to show where your raw materials came from and how each batch was made is part of showing good manufacturing practice. It also helps when you train a helper: she can follow your written record instead of guessing.
Four numbers worth tracking

items: **Yield:** good bars per batch. Tells you whether cutting and moulds are consistent.
**Reject rate:** rejected bars divided by bars cut, times 100. Aim to bring it down batch by batch.
**Cure weight loss:** (weight at cutting minus cured weight) divided by weight at cutting, times 100. Tells you how much heavier to cut bars so the cured weight matches your label.
**Cost per good bar:** total batch cost divided by good bars. You will use this for pricing in Module 4.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading two batches
blocks.context: For example, Chinwe in Onitsha compares batch CH-01 and batch CH-02 of the same recipe.
steps: CH-01: 10 bars cut, 2 rejected for rough edges. Reject rate: 2 / 10 x 100 = 20%.
CH-02: she used a cutting guide. 11 bars cut, 1 rejected. Reject rate: 1 / 11 x 100 = about 9%.
Cure weight loss: marked bars averaged 140 g at cutting and 128 g after 5 weeks. (140 minus 128) / 140 x 100 = about 8.6%.
Her label says 120 g, so her bars are comfortably above label weight. She could cut slightly smaller bars, about 133 g fresh, and still be above 120 g after curing.
blocks.result: Chinwe's records show the cutting guide halved her rejects, and her weight data lets her cut more bars per batch while still meeting her label weight.

blocks.title: The quality improvement loop
items: Plan the batch
Make and record
Cure and test
Review the numbers
Change one thing
blocks.caption: Change only one thing at a time so your records show clearly what made the difference.

blocks.text: A five-line quality report

items: Batch and date: what you made.
Result: bars cut, rejects, pH, cured weight.
Problem: anything that went wrong, with the likely cause.
Action: what you will change next batch.
Evidence: photos and the record page attached.

blocks.text: Review your numbers once a month, not only when something goes wrong. Put your last four batches side by side: is the reject rate falling, is cure weight loss steady, is cost per good bar going up because of oil prices? Small trends are easy to see on paper and easy to miss when you rely on memory. Share the five-line report with a mentor, your cooperative or a fellow maker and ask one question: what would you change?

blocks.title: Number every batch
blocks.text: Use your initials and a running number (RK-001, RK-002). Write the batch number on the curing tray, the label and the record. If a customer complains, you can find the exact record in seconds.

takeaways: Every batch gets a number and a full written record
Track yield, reject rate, cure weight loss and cost per good bar
Cure weight loss tells you how big to cut bars to meet label weight
Change one thing at a time and record the result

activity.title: Complete a batch record and report
steps: Fill in a full batch record for your test batch using the table in this lesson.
Calculate reject rate and cure weight loss from your own numbers.
Write a five-line quality report.
Share it with a friend and ask if they can understand it without your help.
activity.evidence: Your completed batch record and five-line report, with your calculations shown.

quiz.q: After 5 weeks, Esther's marked bars weigh the same as the week before and test at about pH 9. What does this suggest?
options: The bars still have too much water
The bars are cured and the pH is normal
The bars have far too much lye
quiz.explain: Stable weight shows the bars have dried, and pH around 9 to 10 is normal for handmade soap.

quiz.q: Halima finds hard, white, crunchy pockets inside some bars. What should she do?
options: Wash the bars and sell them
Discard the batch safely with gloves
Cure them for one more week and sell
quiz.explain: Crunchy white pockets suggest undissolved caustic soda. The batch is not safe to sell.

quiz.q: Which label line is acceptable for a cosmetic soap?
options: Handmade with shea butter and palm oil
quiz.explain: Describing honest ingredients is fine. Cure and infection claims are medicinal, and "chemical free" is untrue.

quiz.q: Bars weigh 150 g at cutting and 135 g after curing. What is the cure weight loss?
According to NAFDAC's MSME page, what is the first document a micro soap maker should get in place?
quiz.explain: NAFDAC accepts evidence of a registered business name for MSMEs, and CAC registration is listed among micro-scale requirements.

quiz.q: Chinwe cut 12 bars and rejected 3. What is her reject rate?

modules.title: Costing, Selling and Growing Your Soap Business
modules.overview: Good soap only becomes a business when every bar is costed correctly, priced with a real profit, presented well and sold to people who come back. This module walks you through costing in naira, pricing, packaging and selling on WhatsApp and in your community, and finishes with your capstone batch record, safety report and 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Costing a batch and pricing each bar for profit
objectives: Calculate the full cost of one batch, including packaging and overheads
Work out cost per good bar, including your own time
Set retail and wholesale prices that leave a profit
Calculate how many bars you must sell to recover your start-up costs

blocks.text: Many small makers price by guessing or by copying the seller next door. Then they discover, months later, that they were working for free. The fix is simple arithmetic you can do on your phone calculator. All naira figures in this lesson are **approximate examples**. Prices change quickly, so always use your own current market prices.

blocks.name: money-bag
blocks.caption: Profit is only what remains after ingredients, packaging, overheads and your labour are paid.

blocks.text: The four layers of cost

items: **Ingredients:** every oil, caustic soda, fragrance, colour, weighed per batch.
**Packaging:** wrapping paper or box, label, sticker, nylon or bag.
**Overheads:** a fair share of gas or fuel, water, gloves, pH strips, transport to the market, data for marketing.
**Labour:** your own time. If you do not pay yourself, the business is not really making money.

blocks.text: Ingredient cost from purchase price

To cost an ingredient, divide what you paid by the quantity you bought, then multiply by what you used. For example, if a 25 litre keg of palm oil costs a certain amount, find the cost per gram by weighing a known volume once, or ask the seller for the weight. Write down the cost per gram of each ingredient on a price sheet and update it whenever you restock.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a 10-bar batch
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Lagos costs her 1,000 g oil batch from Lesson 2.2. These prices are approximate and for illustration only.
steps: Ingredients: palm oil 500 g about 1,500 naira; palm kernel oil 300 g about 1,200 naira; shea butter 150 g about 900 naira; castor oil 50 g about 500 naira; caustic soda 142 g about 400 naira; fragrance 30 g about 1,500 naira. Total about 6,000 naira.
Packaging: 10 printed paper wraps at about 150 naira each (1,500 naira) plus 10 labels at about 50 naira each (500 naira). Total about 2,000 naira.
Overheads share: gas, water, gloves and transport, about 1,000 naira.
Batch cost before labour: 6,000 + 2,000 + 1,000 = 9,000 naira. With 10 good bars: 900 naira per bar.
Labour: 3 hours of making, cutting and wrapping at 1,000 naira per hour = 3,000 naira, or 300 naira per bar.
Full cost per bar: 900 + 300 = 1,200 naira.
blocks.result: Each bar really costs Amaka about 1,200 naira. Any price below that loses money, even if bars sell quickly.

blocks.title: What a soap price is made of
items: Profit
Labour
Overheads
Packaging
Ingredients
blocks.caption: Build the price from the bottom up; profit is only what is left after every layer below is paid.

blocks.text: Setting the price

Decide the profit margin you want, as a share of the selling price. A simple formula is **price = full cost divided by (1 minus margin)**. For a 40% margin on a 1,200 naira cost: 1,200 / 0.60 = 2,000 naira. Then check the market: what do similar handmade bars sell for near you? If yours sits in that range and your quality and label are strong, keep it. If the market will not pay your price, reduce cost (cheaper fragrance, simpler wrap, bigger batches) rather than cutting your profit to nothing.

head: Price type
Example price (approximate)
Profit per bar
rows: Wholesale to a shop (20% off retail)

blocks.text: Break-even on your start-up costs

Your scale, goggles, moulds, blender and pots are a one-time start-up cost. Divide that cost by the profit per bar to find how many bars you must sell to get it back. For example, with 30,000 naira of equipment and 800 naira profit per retail bar: 30,000 / 800 = 37.5, so about 38 bars. That is four batches of 10 bars, which helps you set a realistic first sales target.

Review your prices every time you restock. Oil and fragrance prices in Nigerian markets can rise sharply within a few months, and a price that gave a good margin in January may barely cover cost by June. If you must raise prices, tell regular customers in advance, explain the reason in one honest sentence, and keep quality the same.

blocks.title: Bigger batches lower cost
blocks.text: Overheads and labour do not double when the batch doubles. Once your recipe is reliable, making 2,000 g or 3,000 g of oils at a time usually lowers cost per bar. Re-run the lye calculator for every new batch size.

blocks.title: Do not forget unsold and rejected bars
blocks.text: If 1 bar in 10 is rejected, your cost per good bar rises. Use your real reject rate from your batch records, not a perfect batch, when you price.

takeaways: Cost every batch in four layers: ingredients, packaging, overheads, labour
Full cost per bar = batch cost divided by good bars
Price = full cost divided by (1 minus your margin), then check the market
Break-even bars = start-up cost divided by profit per bar

activity.title: Build your costing sheet
steps: List every ingredient you used with what you paid and how much you used, at today's market prices.
Add packaging, an overheads share and your labour at an hourly rate you choose.
Calculate full cost per good bar using your real number of good bars.
Set a retail and a wholesale price and calculate your break-even number of bars.
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet (paper photo or spreadsheet) showing every line and the final prices.

lessons.title: Packaging, branding and selling on WhatsApp and locally
objectives: Choose packaging that protects bars and shows your label
Take clear product photos with a phone
Set up a WhatsApp Business catalogue and a simple sales routine
Receive payments safely and avoid common payment scams

blocks.text: People buy soap with their eyes and their nose first, then come back because of how it feels in use. Your job is to make the first purchase easy and the second purchase likely. You do not need an expensive brand agency. You need neat packaging, honest information, good photos and reliable service.

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.alt: A seller chatting with a customer on a phone
blocks.caption: Quick, friendly WhatsApp replies turn an enquiry into a sale and a repeat customer.

blocks.text: Packaging that works

items: **Only wrap cured bars.** Wrapping fresh soap traps moisture and can cause sweating and spots.
**Paper wraps or kraft boxes** let the soap breathe and look natural. Shrink wrap keeps scent in but can trap moisture in humid weather; test it first.
**One clear label** on every bar: name, ingredients, net weight, batch number, dates, contact.
**Consistent look:** same colours, font and logo on every product so customers recognise you on a shop shelf or a WhatsApp status.

blocks.text: Naming and branding

Choose a short brand name that is easy to say, spell and search on WhatsApp, and check that no one nearby already uses it. If you plan to register with NAFDAC and grow, consider registering the name as a business name with CAC and, later, as a trademark. Pick two brand colours and one font and use them on labels, price lists and Status posts. Name each product by what it is, for example "Lemongrass Shea Bar", so customers know what they are buying without asking.
Photos with your phone

items: Shoot in daylight near a window, not under a yellow bulb, and switch off the flash.
Use a plain background: white paper, a wooden board or a clean cloth.
Take three shots of each soap: the wrapped bar with label, the cut bar showing its colour, and a lather shot in hands.
Keep the phone steady and wipe the camera lens first. Crop, but do not use filters that change the soap's true colour.

blocks.text: Selling on WhatsApp Business

The free WhatsApp Business app lets you create a business profile with your address and hours, a **catalogue** of products with photos and prices, quick replies for common questions, and labels to organise customers (for example "new", "paid", "delivered"). Post on your Status regularly: a new batch curing, a customer's happy message (with permission), a short video of cutting a loaf. Ask satisfied customers to share your catalogue link.

Do not rely on one channel. Many soap makers also sell at church or mosque events, women's association meetings, salons, and small supermarkets. Offer a small sample or a cut tester bar at stalls so people can smell and feel the soap.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 30-second pitch and a weekly routine
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze in Port Harcourt has 30 cured bars and wants to sell them within three weeks at 2,000 naira each (approximate).
steps: Her pitch: "I make small-batch bar soap with palm oil, palm kernel oil and shea butter, cured for five weeks so it lasts longer. Each bar is 120 g, 2,000 naira, unscented or lemongrass."
Monday: she posts the catalogue link and three photos on Status and sends it to 20 contacts personally.
Wednesday: she posts a lather video. Friday: she takes 10 bars and two testers to her women's group meeting.
She records every enquiry and sale in a notebook with date and channel, and confirms each payment in her bank or Opay app before sending soap.
At the end of week three she counts: 26 bars sold, 4 left for her next market day.
blocks.result: Adaeze sold 26 bars (about 52,000 naira, approximate) and her notebook shows which channel brought most sales, so she knows where to spend time next month.

blocks.title: From stranger to repeat buyer
items: Sees photo or tester
Asks on WhatsApp
Pays and confirms
Receives and uses
Reorders or refers
blocks.caption: Each step needs a quick, friendly response; slow replies lose sales.

blocks.text: Delivery and after-sales care

Agree delivery fees before payment, and use dispatch riders or park transport you trust for orders outside your area. Pack bars in a small carton or paper bag so they do not get crushed. Two or three days after delivery, send a short message asking how the customer likes the soap. This simple follow-up brings honest feedback for your records, catches problems early, and often leads to a reorder or a referral. Keep a list of repeat customers and offer them first access to new batches.

blocks.title: Protect yourself from payment scams
blocks.text: Fake bank alerts and edited payment screenshots are common. Release goods only after you see the money in your own banking, Opay or Moniepoint app, not from an SMS or screenshot the customer sends. Payment links from services such as Paystack also confirm payment for you. Never share your PIN or one-time code with anyone, including people claiming to be from your bank.

blocks.title: Customer data
blocks.text: Keep customer phone numbers and addresses private. Do not add people to broadcast lists or groups without their permission, and let them opt out easily.

takeaways: Wrap only cured bars, in packaging that breathes and shows your label
Daylight, plain background, three photos per soap
Use the WhatsApp Business catalogue, Status and quick replies, plus in-person sales
Confirm payment in your own app before releasing goods

activity.title: Launch your mini shop
steps: Take three daylight photos of one cured, labelled bar.
Set up a WhatsApp Business profile and add the soap to your catalogue with price and description.
Write and practise a 30-second pitch.
Share the catalogue with 10 people and record every response for one week.
